findings.title: Negative-offset slicing in OptimizedCursorPaginator silently returns wrong rows or raises IndexError
findings.body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (e.g. `queryset[-5:96]`). Django QuerySets do NOT support negative slicing — this raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` at query evaluation time, turning any request with a negative cursor offset into a 500 error. Even if it were supported (e.g. on a list), negative slicing counts from the END of the result set, which would return the wrong rows entirely (the last N rows of the table rather than rows before the cursor), corrupting pagination results. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong. Additionally, the cursor value is attacker-controlled via the `cursor` query parameter, so any client of the audit log endpoint passing `optimized_pagination=true` with a crafted negative-offset cursor triggers this. The negative-offset branch must be removed or replaced with a correct reverse-pagination implementation.

findings.title: BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative offsets to 0, breaking prev-cursor pagination and enabling duplicate rows
findings.body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters existing behavior for ALL paginators using BasePaginator (Paginator, DateTimePaginator, etc.), not just the new one. Previously `queryset[offset:stop]` with a negative offset would raise Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' error; now a negative offset is silently clamped to 0, so the query restarts from the beginning of the dataset. Cursor offsets are derived from client-supplied cursor strings (`Cursor.from_string` parses `int(bits[1])` with no validation), so a client can send a cursor with a negative offset and receive the first page of results while the returned next/prev cursors are computed from those wrong results — producing duplicated rows across pages and inconsistent pagination state. This is a data-integrity regression in a shared, core pagination path used by many endpoints. Negative offsets should be rejected with BadPaginationError (as OffsetPaginator and ChainPaginator already do), not clamped.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator prev-page trimming uses unclamped negative offset in length comparison
findings.body: In the `cursor.is_prev and cursor.value` branch, the code checks `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:` where `offset = cursor.offset` can be negative (the new code path explicitly allows negative offsets). With a negative offset this comparison can never be true when it should be, or can be true when it should not, so the extra fetched row is not trimmed correctly — resulting in an off-by-one row appearing (or disappearing) at the boundary of reverse pagination. The comparison should use the actual `start_offset` used for the slice, not the raw (possibly negative) `offset`.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the audit log endpoint orders by '-datetime'
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The endpoint wires it with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key == "datetime"` and `value` is a `datetime` object — `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, so every paginated request through this paginator crashes with a 500. The class is a copy of `Paginator` (integer keys) and was never adapted to datetime keys; it should subclass/reuse `DateTimePaginator`'s key handling (millisecond conversion via `strftime("%s.%f")` and `value_from_cursor` converting back with `datetime.fromtimestamp`), otherwise the 'optimized' path is entirely broken for the only endpoint that uses it.

findings.title: Undocumented, unvalidated query parameter gates a different paginator based on superuser/global-access status
findings.body: `use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"` introduces a hidden, undocumented API parameter that switches the response's pagination behavior (different paginator class, different cursor semantics) for superusers and members with global access. Because the two paginators produce different cursor formats and edge-case behavior (and the optimized one is broken — see other findings), clients that cache or persist cursors across requests can get inconsistent results. More importantly, the parameter is not declared in any serializer or API documentation, so it is invisible to API consumers and to schema generation, and the `enable_advanced_features=True` flag is passed unconditionally whenever the user is privileged — there is no way to opt out per-request. Feature-gating pagination internals on a raw query-string flag is a contract hazard; the paginator choice should be deterministic per endpoint, not client-controlled.

findings.title: AttributeError risk: organization_context.member may be None, and has_global_access is not a documented field
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` without a None check. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is an optional RPC field (it is None when the request is not authenticated as an organization member, e.g. certain internal/service or staff flows that still reach this endpoint), which would raise `AttributeError` and return a 500 instead of a paginated response. Additionally, `has_global_access` is not a standard field on the member RPC model used elsewhere in this codebase (global access is typically determined via `OrganizationMember` flags / `has_global_access` on the ORM model or via `organization_context.flags`), so this check may silently never grant access or may not exist on the RPC type at all — it needs verification against the actual RPC schema.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim duplicate of BasePaginator.get_result with no actual optimization
findings.body: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` (lines 845-911) duplicates `BasePaginator.get_result` almost line-for-line, including the same `count_hits` subquery, the same `extra` row fetch, and the same slicing strategy. The only behavioral differences are the broken negative-offset branch and the broken datetime key handling. There is no performance optimization present — no keyset/seek pagination (the `build_queryset` range filter is identical to the base class), no deferred `count_hits`, no `only()`/`values()` projection. Shipping a duplicate ~70-line method that claims 'optimized query path for large datasets' in its docstring is misleading and adds maintenance surface for zero benefit; either implement a real optimization (e.g. seek/keyset pagination on (datetime, id)) or delete the class and use DateTimePaginator.

findings.title: Pre-existing typo `queryset.query.order_b` introduced/preserved in ordering-reversal path
findings.body: Line 105 assigns `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — the attribute is `order_by`, not `order_b`. This is in the `elif ("-%s" % self.key) in queryset.query.order_by:` branch of `build_queryset`, which executes when a queryset already ordered by `-key` is paginated with an ascending (prev-page) cursor. The assignment silently sets a nonexistent attribute, so the intended ordering reversal never happens and the queryset keeps its original `-key` ordering — producing incorrectly ordered results for prev-cursor pagination on pre-ordered querysets. This path is reachable from the audit log endpoint (queryset ordered by `-datetime` via `order_by="-datetime"` combined with a prev cursor).

findings.title: Comment claims negative offsets are allowed, but Cursor.from_string and all paginators reject or mishandle them
findings.body: The added comment states 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but nothing in `Cursor` validates or specially handles negative offsets: `from_string` happily parses them, `OffsetPaginator.get_result` raises `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")` for them, `ChainPaginator` and `CombinedQuerysetPaginator` do the same, and `BasePaginator` now silently clamps them to 0 (see other finding). The comment documents behavior that does not exist and contradicts the rest of the codebase; it should be removed or replaced with an explicit statement that negative offsets are invalid.

findings.body: The PR adds a new paginator class, a new endpoint branch keyed on `optimized_pagination=true` and user privilege, and modifies the shared `BasePaginator.get_result` slicing logic — but includes no tests. Existing paginator tests (tests/sentry/api/test_paginator.py) and audit log endpoint tests (tests/sentry/api/endpoints/test_organization_auditlogs.py) are untouched, so the regressions described in the other findings (negative-offset clamping in BasePaginator, TypeError on datetime keys, AssertionError on negative slicing) would all pass CI. At minimum, tests are needed for: BasePaginator with a negative-offset cursor (must raise, not clamp), OptimizedCursorPaginator with a datetime-ordered queryset, and the audit log endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` for superuser vs regular member.
